native_result.query: How is the advantage in BA degree completion rates for Black students related to Socioeconomic status levels?
native_result.HypoA: The advantage in BA degree completion rates for Black students is more pronounced at lower SES levels with the interaction term for Socioeconomic status and being black having a coefficient of 0.7606
native_result.HypoB: BA completion is not measurable in this extract (no degree/diploma variable exists anywhere in nls_raw.csv), so the analysis uses a college-PARTICIPATION proxy: ever recorded in residence type 3 (DORM/FRATERNITY/SORORITY) in waves 1981-1996, or already >=16 grades completed in 1979. On this proxy the Black vs non-Black non-Hispanic difference is SES-conditional, not a constant advantage. At the lowest family-of-origin SES level (index from parental occupation white/blue at 14, mother's and father's grades, per-capita family net income 1979) Black and comparison respondents participate at statistically indistinguishable rates (4.0% vs 3.4%, +0.6pp, 95% CI -0.9..+2.2; +3.5pp, p=0.0001 once sex and ASVAB achievement are held constant); at the middle level the gap is -3.0pp; at the highest level -7.9pp (11.4% vs 19.3%). The Black-minus-comparison gap therefore widens by about -7.6 percentage points per +1 SD of the origin-SES index (CI -9.0..-6.1; relative scale OR 0.46 per SD, 0.36-0.58; logit interaction joint Wald p=0.0165). Hypothesis: rising family socioeconomic status converts into college participation far less efficiently for Black students than for their non-Black non-Hispanic peers, so any Black advantage is confined to the lowest-SES families, is not distinguishable from parity in the raw data, and is extinguished and then reversed as SES rises. Level-specific Black cells at high SES are small (237 respondents, 27 events, 80%-power MDE 7.5pp), so only the direction of the SES-by-race trend is well powered; the pattern replicates across occupation cut-points (400/500/600), quartiles, an index without occupation, complete-case and >=2-component indices, age strata addressing right-censoring, and an 'all non-Black' comparison. Since the outcome is enrollment and not degree receipt, and no sampling weights exist (all Black respondents come from oversample strata), no claim about BA degree completion rates is supported by this file.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Verified absence of any degree/SES variable (keyword scan of column names and all cell values; datasheet-vs-file diff). 2) Built outcome proxy college = ever residence==3 (1981-96) OR grade79>=16; dorm_only reported separately (OR adds 37 cases). 3) Built origin-SES z-index (parental occupation white/blue at code<500, mother/father grades winsorised at 16, log per-capita family net income 1979; >=3 of 4 components) and cut tertiles (quartiles as sensitivity). 4) Per-level n, events, Wilson CIs, Newcombe difference CIs, Katz log-RR CIs, small-cell flags (n<100, events<10). 5) Logit college ~ SES_level x Black (joint Wald) + LPM black*SES_z with HC1 (absolute-scale trend) + logit black*SES_z (relative-scale trend) + net Black effects per level adjusted for male and ASVAB. 6) Power: level-specific two-proportion post-hoc power and 80%-power MDE. 7) Sensitivities: occupation thresholds 400/500/600 with white-collar shares by race, occupation-missing-as-category + no-occupation index + complete-case + >=2-component index, logistic model of occupation missingness on race, age strata (14-16, 17-19, 18-22, 20-22) for censoring, quartiles, all-non-Black comparison, HS-by-1979 risk set, endogenous own-wealth inclusion, plus descriptive wealth/income context table and option-C grade distribution. Executed: analysis/main_analysis.py (exit 0) -> analysis/report.txt.

sub_hypo.text: Rising family-of-origin socioeconomic status is associated with a substantially smaller increase in college participation for Black respondents than for non-Black non-Hispanic respondents. Degree completion is not measurable. Analyses are unweighted because sampling weights are absent; all Black respondents are from oversample strata. sub_hypo.relations: Race moderates the association between origin SES and college participation. The standardized SES index uses white/blue-collar parental occupation at code <500, maternal and paternal grades winsorised at 16, and log per-capita family net income, requiring at least three of four components. The raw Black-minus-comparison participation gap is +0.6 percentage points at low SES (4.0% versus 3.4%; 95% CI -0.9 to +2.2), -3.0 points at middle SES, and -7.9 points at high SES (11.4% versus 19.3%). Adjusting for sex and ASVAB achievement yields a low-SES Black advantage of +3.5 points (p=0.0001). The gap becomes 7.6 points more negative per one-SD increase in SES (95% CI -9.0 to -6.1); the relative-scale interaction OR is 0.46 per SD (95% CI 0.36–0.58), with joint logit interaction Wald p=0.0165. The trend replicates across occupation cut-points 400/500/600, SES quartiles, an index without occupation, complete-case and at-least-two-component indices, age strata addressing right-censoring, and an all-non-Black comparison. These relationships concern participation, not BA completion.
